title: Earl Humphrey and how his own tone and vibrato developed
summary: He never heard Earl Humphrey, then explains how his tone and vibrato changed, a union anecdote and his continued practice.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Did you ever hear Earl Humphrey play?
No, I never did. And I'm sad about that because you see the thing-
Even as a kid you never heard of?

No. Earl was playing way before me, you know. He played with Emmanuel Perez around 1915. See I didn't leave here until 1917 with my parents. But I still had, I used to pass by the Humphreys, you know, and here they played. I saw the grandfather and the father.
They still had Cadiz and Liberty.

Yeah, same place. And right around on Jenna I think it was, the two hall boys, they're the cousins to the Humphreys, you know. And I used to see them carrying the instruments. But still, I never thought about playing in the music, you see. And so you take, for instance, the vibrato you spoke about. I used to get more or less a straight tone, you understand. And when I first noticed that my tone was changing, I get more of a vibrato now than ever. I got that, I started that because different trombone players, I liked the tone like Lawrence Brown, I even liked Seagarden, Higginbotham. See, all those fellas, they've always been ranked over me, even Ory. But Ory, not bragging, Ory has never been a trombone player. I am. I'm raised a pretty good musician, you know, all around musician. And I think now I play more of a trombone than he ever played. That's just my opinion. And so I'm with Louie at the Palace in Cleveland. So I'm practicing the dressing room. First was, then we went to Chicago theater, and Chicago was a fellow there in the pit band. I was noodling around in my hand playing a little jazz. And so he came and introduced himself. He wanted to take some lessons for me. So I said, well, the guy like this, I hear him with them big round tones in on him, his bottom notes, boom, triple tongue and all that stuff. I said, well, the guy like this, he wanted to take lessons from me. Well, there's a lot of jealousies, I foresaid, at the union there. Now, Willie Hightower's wife was the financial secretary, see, and she'd throw a few crumbs my way, but otherwise if you didn't go up there and blast those dice and gamble. The guys used to come up there in their tuxedos ready to go to work. They'd go to work and Boyd Hall would go around and pick them up after they finished and bring them up there to gamble and play poker. Well if you didn't go up there and gamble, people would call you up. And unless Miss Hightower got over to it, well, just like this fellow came, you know, came out of the union to see me about taking some lessons. But they told them about another guy and I didn't see him anymore. So I'm in Cleveland and finally I found out I'm doing something wrong. My tunes became broader and I'm getting a little more vibrato. You see what I'm talking about? So now, the way I play now, I use more vibrato than that. Anytime a trumpet player with me, like in the band I've been playing in Chicago, well the leader asked him to use a little more vibrato in order for the match with me. You see, I like it on playing particularly some sweet tune, and I do love to play like tune like getting sentimental over you and things like that you know. And I'm striving right as of yet. I'm still trying, I'm striving for intonation. I mean I'm 71 years old but I still figure I can improve. I am improving. See what I'm talking about? I am improving. And I figure there isn't as much as I intend to play music most likely until I die. Well why not try to get better?
